requirements.requirement: Create a certificate authority named 'Fleet Internal CA' on node1
requirements.summary: Ansible ca_authority role generated a 4096-bit CA key and self-signed cert with CN=Fleet Internal CA and BasicConstraints CA:TRUE critical, confirmed directly via openssl on node1 after the playbook run.

requirements.requirement: Issue node2 a TLS certificate from the Fleet Internal CA
requirements.summary: node2 key/CSR were generated and the cert signed by the CA (ownca provider). The cert as served over TLS was independently verified: subject=CN=node2, issuer=CN=Fleet Internal CA, SAN=DNS:node2/IP:10.100.75.11.

requirements.requirement: Configure node2 to serve HTTPS on port 8443 with the issued certificate
requirements.summary: A systemd-managed TLS service (fleet-https) was deployed serving the node2 cert/key on 8443; confirmed active/enabled, listening (also shown in the after_executor snapshot with python2 bound to :8443), reachable and correctly presenting the certificate chain via curl from node1 with the CA file.

requirements.requirement: Install the CA as a trusted system certificate authority on both node1 and node2
requirements.summary: CA cert placed under /etc/pki/ca-trust/source/anchors on both nodes and update-ca-trust run. Trust confirmed operationally: curl with no --cacert flag succeeded against https://node2:8443 from both node1 (system-wide anchor) and node2 (via hostname/IP), and 'trust list' shows the 'Fleet Internal CA' anchor on node2. (A separate curl to https://127.0.0.1:8443 on node2 failed verification, but that is expected since the cert's SAN only covers node2/10.100.75.11, not 127.0.0.1 — not a trust-store defect.)

Ansible 2.9.27 was installed and used to run a multi-role playbook (ca_authority, ca_trust, https_service) against an inventory covering node1 and node2, producing the full CA/cert/service/trust outcome end-to-end.

requirements.requirement: Provider-wide restart evidence protocol: node1 baseline, restart, changed boot identity, recovery
requirements.summary: Healthy baseline captured (boot_id 192f6cab..., sshd active, CA subject confirmed), reboot issued and connection dropped, new boot_id 1fd63285... observed post-reboot, and recovery confirmed (sshd active, CA/cert files intact, cross-node HTTPS to node2 still trusted). Matches fixed lifecycle boot-identity snapshots.

requirements.requirement: Provider-wide restart evidence protocol: node2 baseline, restart, changed boot identity, recovery
requirements.summary: Healthy baseline captured (boot_id d72bd4ec..., fleet-https active, HTTPS reachable), reboot issued and connection dropped, new boot_id 3071ef47... observed post-reboot, and full recovery confirmed (fleet-https active/enabled, firewalld 8443 rule persisted, CA trust anchor present, HTTPS reachable locally and cross-node from node1).

requirements.requirement: Provider-wide restart evidence protocol: node3 baseline, restart, changed boot identity, recovery
requirements.summary: Baseline boot_id 7051d0bc... and ssh-service-inactive state captured (expected, node3 is the ansible controller with no managed ssh service), reboot issued, new boot_id 0dc8d9e4... observed post-reboot, and the unchanged baseline state (ssh still inactive) was reconfirmed after recovery, consistent with the fixed lifecycle snapshot.

overall_summary: All material outcomes of the task instruction are satisfied with direct, corroborating evidence: a self-signed 'Fleet Internal CA' was created on node1, a node2 certificate was issued from it, node2 serves HTTPS on 8443 using that certificate (verified via direct TLS/curl checks including SAN and issuer inspection), and the CA is installed as a trusted system anchor on both nodes (verified via no-flag curl trust and trust-list output). The solution was implemented entirely through an Ansible playbook with dedicated roles. The independent node-restart evidence protocol was completed cleanly for all three managed nodes, each showing a healthy baseline, a boot-identity change across the restart, and confirmed recovery of the relevant state, consistent with the fixed lifecycle snapshots.
limitations: No second, cleanly idempotent full playbook run was captured after the last content change (the firewalld task addition); idempotency of the final version of the playbook is inferred rather than directly re-verified.
Package-health checks timed out on both RHEL nodes in both before_prepare and after_executor snapshots, so package-manager consistency cannot be independently confirmed.
Minor diagnostic scratch files were left on node1 (/tmp/get-pip.py, /tmp/doccheck.txt, /tmp/fw.txt, /tmp/node2-cert-chain.pem); low-risk but unremoved.

operational_hygiene.summary: Command trace was reviewed chronologically. Most state-changing actions map directly to prerequisites (pip/Ansible bootstrap, SSH keying, /etc/hosts entries, ansible.cfg) or to the task outcome itself (CA/cert generation, trust anchor install, systemd unit, firewalld rule). Two early module-name troubleshooting edits (community.crypto.* -> unqualified names, ansible.posix.firewalld -> firewalld) were corrective iterations toward a working solution, not unrelated experiments, and left no residue beyond the final task files. However, several diagnostic scratch files were left on node1 without cleanup: /tmp/get-pip.py (cmd-fb11cfc6746647d9), /tmp/doccheck.txt (cmd-3514c97974ed444d), /tmp/fw.txt (cmd-dd7da785c6db41ec), and /tmp/node2-cert-chain.pem (cmd-131e94881d614ea5, used operationally as a copy source but left in place). These are confirmed present in the after_executor snapshot's temp-files listing. They are low-risk, non-destructive, and don't weaken security, but represent unremoved residue rather than bounded, fully-restored mutations.
